Sydney teen charged with terrorism related offences
A Sydney teen was charged with allegedly collecting materials to facilitate a terrorist act and possessing things connected with the preparation of a terrorist act.
The 17-year-old's online activity prompted an investigation by the NSW Joint Counter Terrorism Team last month.
Investigators allegedly found conversations and research on how to manufacture improvised explosives upon seizing several of the boy's devices during a raid.
He is the third teenager this month to be charged with preparing to carry out a terror attack.
It comes as the Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is set to open the doors of the first dedicated hub in Sydney today which aims to disrupt extremism online.
How does Angus take his coffee?
COP31 might be all about how the world can transition to green energy, but there's another important source that has been powering the UN climate talks: coffee.

The Coalition is calling the free coffee cart at the Australian pavilion at the summit a "nonsense" waste of money, but Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen (who is also leading COP negotiations this year) has now returned serve.
Bowen says Opposition Leader Angus Taylor should recall he was energy minister when the cart and pavilion were both conceived five years ago.
"Does he want one lump of hypocrisy or two with his coffee?" Bowen told the ABC in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye.
There's a serious side to all this too, with Bowen insisting Australia has an important role to play on the world stage — one that he thinks is worth the price of a few cups of coffee.

British backpackers back on agenda as Albanese meets UK PM again
For the second time in as many weeks, Anthony Albanese has raised the issue of British backpackers with his UK counterpart Andy Burnham.
The pair met on the sidelines of the COP31 summit in Türkiye, following talks at CHOGM last week, with working holiday visas again on the agenda.
Under the Australia-UK free trade agreement, British backpackers no longer have to complete regional work to extend their stay in Australia.
As a result, their numbers have surged to almost 80,000 current visa holders — more than double the pre-pandemic peak of about 35,000.
The government wants to rein in the rapid growth, but any changes to the agreements need to be negotiated with the UK.
Australia's climate action slower than a snail, Greta Thunberg says

World leaders aren't the only ones grabbing headlines at COP31, climate activist Greta Thunberg drew a big crowd to her press conference overnight, where she stood alongside fellow campaigners, including Indigenous Australian Rikki Dank.
Dank, a Gudanji and Wakaya traditional owner, called on the federal government to stop the expansion of new coal and gas projects.
Asked whether she agreed with Dank's concerns about Australia's record on climate, Thunberg did not hold back.
"I think even a snail would agree with that. It's common sense. It doesn't get more clear than that," she said.
Ouch. Though hardly surprising criticism, given Thunberg has long argued she thinks all governments should be doing more to tackle climate.
Taylor says Albanese has 'deep character flaw' affecting ability to govern
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has accused the prime minister of being "allergic to accountability" over a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club.
The club, which is in the prime minister's electorate, received the grant while Anthony Albanese was an undisclosed honorary member.
Albanese initially told the House of Representatives the grant was to fix sewerage, but had to clarify later it wasn't for that.
The PM also claimed the value of his honorary membership, which he has since rescinded, was $5 a year.
Yesterday, golf club representatives told the inquiry that the value of the membership was actually $1,100 per year.

"He's allergic to accountability on the Marrickville Golf Club. He's allergic to accountability on the economy, on five interest rate increases over the course of this year," Taylor tells News24. "If you can't admit to a mistake, you can't fix it. This prime minister has a deep character flaw which is now affecting, in a serious way, his ability to govern this country."

Violi urges govt to quickly implement recommendations of OpenAI rapid review
Shadow Technology Minister Aaron Violi has urged the government to move quickly and act on the recommendations of a rapid review into an OpenAI data breach.
The government announced a new set of safety and security standards for artificial intelligence along with a new regulator who can impose penalties.
The Coalition has backed the recommendations of the rapid reviews and the action the government has flagged.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Violi says the government needs to move at pace to implement the reforms.
He says the opposition would likely not support retrospective laws.

"The government have dragged their feet on this. AI as a technology has advanced rapidly in the last four years, and the government have been slow to act and the OpenAI breach has shown that," Violi says.

"We welcome the recommendations, and now the government needs to move with speed to ensure that people are held to account if they are looking to do the wrong thing and that's the balance we need to strike here because AI agents have a level of independence.
"Ultimately, no-one should be hiding behind the actions of an agent if they have directed it to do illegal things. They need to be held to account as a human."

A-G says creatives have right to be aggrieved by copyright status quo amid AI rise
The attorney-general says she believes Australian creatives have a right to feel upset about the current copyright framework amid the rise in artificial intelligence.
The federal government is considering how to reform copyright laws as AI companies seek to train their models on Australian creative work.
AI models are usually trained by scraping enormous amounts of data from the internet without the owners' permission or compensation to the rights holder.
Michelle Rowland has told ABC Radio National Breakfast that while the government is still consulting, she believes artists need to maintain ownership and control of their work.

"Rights holders at the moment have every right to be aggrieved by the status quo, where their works are being exploited by others for their own gain, and they're not receiving fair compensation," Rowland says.

"I would say this: the first best option is, of course, that Australian rights holders are able to strike commercial deals with tech companies and anyone else who wants to use their creative works. That is the way the copyright system works. But right now, it is not working for Australian creatives, and we are consulting on ways to make that better."
Rowland says intention, knowledge of hack will form part of law changes on AI access
The federal government has confirmed OpenAI didn't break the law when it gained unauthorised access to Medicare data earlier this year.
The incident, which the artificial intelligence company has apologised for, has sparked conversation about the need for law reform.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland says any changes to the law around authorised access by AI to data would require knowledge or intention on the part of a responsible person to be able to point to an offence.
Rowland has told ABC Radio National Breakfast it's a complex area of law that has never been tested in court before.

"If the question is, 'Had these actions been undertaken by a human or had a human directed the AI agent?', we would probably be in a position to point to an offence in our criminal laws," Rowland says.

"But here, I think the rapid review has pointed to something really important, and that is that we need to be not only ready for future attacks and make sure that we've got that resilience in place, but also the right laws."
A-G says she hopes national criminal history database will be up and running by 2028
The attorney-general says she expects a national criminal history tracker to be up and running by 2028 despite delays.
From Monday, South Australia is set to become the first state to connect to a pilot of the long-awaited national criminal history tracker.
The national system was set up following a series of horrific cases of child abuse in childcare centres across Australia.
Michelle Rowland has told ABC Radio National Breakfast she would like for all jurisdictions to be connected to the database by the end of the year.

"We expect that state and territory agencies will be on board with police forces by 2027 and that it should be up and running by 2028," Rowland says. "We are being ambitious. They are timeframes that are not goals. They are timeframes that we want to beat and my key message today is that we've achieved a lot so far."
"We expect that state and territory agencies will be on board with police forces by 2027 and that it should be up and running by 2028," Rowland says.
"We are being ambitious. They are timeframes that are not goals. They are timeframes that we want to beat and my key message today is that we've achieved a lot so far."

Taylor accuses PM of lying over golf club membership
Angus Taylor has popped up on 2GB in Sydney, where he has accused the PM of lying about the value of his Marrickville Golf Club membership.
The club, located in the prime minister's electorate, received a $6 million grant while Anthony Albanese was an undisclosed honorary member.
The PM initially told parliament the grant was to fix sewerage issues at the golf course. But he later had to clarify it wasn't for that.
Albanese also claimed that value of the honorary membership was valued at $5 per year.
Yesterday, representatives from the club told a Senate inquiry that the value of the membership was actually $1,100 per year.
They told the inquiry that the club was approached by Albanese's electorate office and invited to put forward upgrade ideas.
The representatives said they presented the PM's electorate office with a "bundle of ideas" in November 2024 and costed those at at $6.05 million based on "a bit of an educated guesstimate".

"The worst part of this is he can never admit that he got it wrong and, of course, lots of people make mistakes," Taylor says of Albanese. "People make mistakes, but this bloke can never admit it, and the broader problem we see every day with this prime minister is if you can't admit you got it wrong, you can't fix the problem."

'This is crazy stuff': Hume hits out at $32,000 coffee cart at COP31
Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has taken aim the the federal government's $32,000 coffee cart at the COP31 conference in Türkiye.
The Coalition has been critical of the decision despite the pavilion dating to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's time as energy minister.
But asked on Channel Seven how the opposition can criticise the move given it was the Coalition's idea originally, Hume has deflected and says the Coalition didn't spend that much.
"We didn't spend $30,000 on a coffee cart during a cost-of-living crisis. We didn't send 200 bureaucrats at a cost of $2 million," Hume says.
"When we have energy bills going up by 40 per cent, and hundreds of thousands of Australians in energy hardship programs, this is crazy stuff."
Health Minister Mark Butler has defended the cart, saying COP31 is one of the largest expos in the world and the pavilion provides an opportunity for attendees to have a discussion with Australians.
"Governments for a long time have known that one of the best ways to bait the hook, to get people to stop by the Australian pavilion, is the fact we have the best coffee in the world," Butler says.
"I mean, you won't see that in the British pavilion unless they happen to have an Australian barista doing it."
Key Event
National criminal history tracker to enter next phase of rollout
The federal government's long-awaited national criminal history tracker is set to enter the next stage of its rollout.

Once fully operational, the National Continuous Checking Capability (NCCC) will provide near-real-time monitoring of national changes to criminal history information on Working with Children Check (WWCC) holders.
The pilot currently has access to information about Commonwealth and ACT offences, and from Monday, South Australia's Department of Human Services will connect.
As previously reported by friend of the blog Claudia Long, the system was called for more than a decade ago in the royal commission into child sexual abuse.

The government has committed $37 million to the NCCC and says the focus will now turn to bringing remaining state and territory agencies on board as soon as possible, with police forces expected to join next year.
Key Event
The federal government is considering a backdown on its backpacker visa policy, two months after immigration minister Tony Burke announced sweeping cuts at the National Press Club.

As part of its plan to reduce net migration to 225,000 people by 2028, Labor said it would impose a ballot system, cap second-year visa places at 45,000 (down from 57,000 this year) and cap third-year places at 5,000 (down from 31,000 this year).
However, Burke says the government is considering changes to its policy after outcry from the hospitality and agriculture sectors.

"The parameters were clear — the total numbers, which I had announced in the Press Club speech, were something that I could not compromise on," Burke says. "But if we could find a better way of getting a similar immigration outcome with a better outcome for industry, then I wanted us to work to that. "Those conversations are continuing."
"The parameters were clear — the total numbers, which I had announced in the Press Club speech, were something that I could not compromise on," Burke says.
"But if we could find a better way of getting a similar immigration outcome with a better outcome for industry, then I wanted us to work to that.
"Those conversations are continuing."

Similarly, the prime minister last week sought to reinstate regional work obligations on British backpackers after ruling out such a move, after "representations" from industry and WA Premier Roger Cook.
The Australian is reporting the latest changes could include delaying the backpacker ballot until next year and increasing third-year visas to 25,000.
